en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek has no verb; the article alone ties the phrase to 'Father'.
Supplied in English to carry the Greek third-person command.

01.r: Points ahead to the prayer that follows as the pattern to use.
01.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'in this way, so, thus'. Here it looks forward to the words that follow, not back.

02.r: Draws the prayer out of what Jesus has just said about praying.
02.n: Abbott-Smith: a particle of consequence or simple sequence, 'wherefore, therefore, then', which never stands first in a sentence.

03.r: A command to the disciples about how to pray.
03.n: A present imperative, plural. Abbott-Smith notes that the verb is always used of prayer to God (in classical Greek, to gods), and lists this verse.

04.r: The disciples, set apart from those just described.
04.n: The pronoun is written out, which the verb does not need. Abbott-Smith notes that the nominative is used for emphasis or contrast.

06.r: The Father of all who pray these words together.

07.r: The article, in the case of address, links 'in the heavens' to 'Father'.
07.n: Literally 'the (one) in the heavens'. English needs a verb, so the older translations say 'which art' or 'who art'.

09.r: The heavens, as one known whole.

10.r: The dwelling of God above the earth.
10.n: The Greek is plural, as in the phrase this study renders 'the kingdom of the heavens'. Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses the word chiefly for Hebrew שָׁמַיִם, a plural form, and that the Greek is hence often plural. Only the YLT keeps 'heavens'.

11.r: May God's name be honoured as holy.
11.n: An aorist passive imperative, third person: a request that something be done, with no doer named. Abbott-Smith gives the verb as 'to make holy, consecrate, sanctify', first 'to dedicate, separate, set apart for God'. Applied to God's name, a reasonable reading is that it be acknowledged and treated as holy, not that it become holy.

13.r: God's name, standing for God himself as he is known.
13.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew שֵׁם.
